Learning Objectives
Describe the unique pediatric anatomic and physiologic factors that contribute to
development of osteomyelitis.
Identify common pathogens in osteomyelitis based upon patient age and risk factors.
Describe the diagnosis of osteomyelitis using patient history, physical examination, imaging,
and laboratory findings.
Describe the treatment algorithm and surgical indications for osteomyelitis.
Identify and diagnose common complications and sequelae of osteomyelitis.


Demographics/Incidence
Hematogenous osteomyelitis is far more common in children than adults. The incidence
of acute and subacute pediatric osteomyelitis is 13 per 100,000 children,1 with a mean
hospitalization rate of 1.3 to 1.7 per 100,000 children. Osteomyelitis is slightly more
commonly in boys than girls (1.6 to 1.8 male to female ratio). Research from the 1980s
and 1990s demonstrated a higher rate of osteomyelitis in children younger than 3 years;
however, more recent research has shown the highest rates of infections in children
aged 2, 7, and 12 years.2 The overall rate of pediatric osteomyelitis is decreasing in
developed countries over time.3
Risk Factors
Risk factors include trauma, sepsis, bacteremia, immunodeficiency, and sickle cell disease

Risk Factors
Multiple risk factors are associated with osteomyelitis. As many as 30% of children with
pediatric osteomyelitis report antecedent trauma. Children with bacteremia and sepsis
also have an increased risk of osteomyelitis. Immunodeficient children, such as those
with diabetes mellitus, malignancy, HIV, chronic steroid treatment, and malnutrition also
have an increased risk.4 Finally, children with sickle cell disease have an increased risk
because of functional asplenia, impaired complement activity, increased gut
permeability, and the presence of chronic infarcted and necrotic bone.5
Anatomic Considerations

Most commonly occurs in the metaphyseal region of long bones
In joints with an intracapsular metaphysis (proximal femur, proximal humerus, distal lateral
tibia, distal fibula, and proximal radius), hematogenous osteomyelitis can spread, potentially
leading to contiguous septic arthritis.
70% of osteomyelitis occurs in the lower extremity.

Anatomic Considerations
In patients with hematogenous osteomyelitis, the initial site of infection is the
metaphysis. The metaphysis contains an abundant vascular supply and large sinusoids
at the epiphyseal-metaphyseal junction that can slow blood flow and encourage
bacterial growth. In older children, the lack of blood vessels across the physis allows the
physis to act as a protective barrier to prevent the spread of the infection into the
epiphysis; however, transphyseal vessels may persist until 18 months of age. Therefore,
osteomyelitis in young children can quickly spread to the epiphysis and into the adjacent
joint. In joints in which the metaphysis is intracapsular, the infection frequently can
result in septic arthritis. These joints include the proximal femur, proximal humerus,
distal lateral tibia, distal fibula, and proximal radius. Hematogenous osteomyelitis most
commonly affects the long bones, and 70% of cases occur in the lower extremity.6
Microbiology Factors
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in pediatric acute hematogenous
osteomyelitis
The incidence of infection caused by community-acquired methicillin-resistant S aureus (CA-
MRSA) is increasing.
The incidence of infection caused by Haemophilus influenza has decreased dramatically since
the introduction of the H influenza vaccine.
Group B Streptococcus is a common pathogen in neonates and Kingella kingae has been
observed in children younger than 4 years.
Unique pathogens are present in certain patient groups, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa in
patients with a foot puncture wound (specifically if socks are worn), group A Streptococcus in
patients with varicella, and Salmonella in children with sickle cell disease.


Microbiology Factors
S aureus is the most common pathogen in pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis.7
This pathogen uses multiple virulence factors to cause infection, including the excretion
of protein A, which inactivates immunoglobulin G antibodies. S aureus also uses a
capsular polysaccharide to reduce opsonization and phagocytosis. The MecA gene
encodes for a form of penicillin-binding protein that has a low affinity for ß-lactam
antibiotic agents. Panton-Valentine leukocidin is a cytotoxin that is used to lyse white
blood cells and cause tissue necrosis. Recent literature has identified 40 genes that are
substantially associated with the severity of illness in children with S aureus infection.
MRSA isolates often have a greater number of virulence genes than methicillin-sensitive
S aureus (MSSA). Although MRSA often causes a more severe clinical disease, the multiple
virulence genes rather than the antibiotic resistance likely determine the severity of the
clinical course. Severe infection also may be observed in children with infections
secondary to MSSA, depending on the virulence factor profile.8 Children with CA-MRSA
have a higher risk for subperiosteal abscess formation, surgical treatment, deep vein
thrombosis, septic pulmonary emboli, and increased hospital length of stay. The relative
local incidence of MRSA should be considered if empiric antibiotic therapy is initiated for
the management of osteomyelitis. Recent literature demonstrates geographic and
institutional variation in the frequency of infections secondary to MRSA in the United
States.9 For example, in Philadelphia, the incidence of CA-MRSA has increased threefold,
from 11% to 35% between 2000 and 2010;10 however, in Texas, analysis of infections
between 2007 and 2014 revealed a 60% decrease in infections secondary to CA-MRSA.11
Several patient populations are susceptible to unique pathogens that must be
considered in the initial selection of antibiotic coverage for pediatric osteomyelitis.
Group B Streptococcus is a common pathogen in neonates. Group B Streptococcus is part
of the normal bacterial flora of the vagina and anus in women and can be transferred to
the fetus at birth via aspiration of amniotic fluid. K kingae is a gram-negative
coccobacillus that is common in the oropharyngeal flora of children younger than 4
years. It produces a cytotoxin that allows it to colonize the respiratory tract and invade
the blood stream12 (Resource 2) The clinical course in children with osteomyelitis
secondary to K kingae often is less severe, triggering a mild-moderate immune response

(39% of children have a normal C-reactive protein (CRP) level, 85% are afebrile), than
other etiologies of osteomyelitis. Importantly, K kingae often is negative on Gram stain
and may require polymerase chain reaction testing to confirm diagnosis.13 A higher rate
of Salmonella infection (32% of infections) is reported in children with sickle cell disease
than in the typical pediatric population; however, S aureus still is the most common
pathogen in children overall. Children with varicella infection have an increased risk for
infection with group A Streptococcus.14P aeruginosa often is observed in patients with a
history of puncture wounds to the foot while wearing socks. Finally, H influenza
osteomyelitis has been nearly eradicated since the introduction of the H influenza
vaccine in 1992;15 however, the typical choice of empiric antibiotic coverage for gram-
positive bacteria should be broadened in children who are unvaccinated to cover these
gram-negative bacteria.
Pathophysiology
Methods of infection in osteomyelitis include hematogenous spread, direct inoculation, and
contiguous spread from local tissue.
Subacute osteomyelitis often is insidious in onset with milder symptoms.
Unmanaged acute osteomyelitis can result in chronic osteomyelitis, defined by the presence of
a sequestrum.
Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO), also known as chronic nonbacterial
osteomyelitis is a noninfectious, inflammatory-mediated form of osteomyelitis.

Pathophysiology
Bacteria can spread to the bone via three routes: hematogenous spread, contiguous
spread, and direct inoculation. The most common route is hematogenous spread, and a
spectrum of disease severity, from transient bacteremia in otherwise healthy children to
sepsis in critically ill children, exists. Osteomyelitis also can result from contiguous
spread from surrounding soft tissues and from direct inoculation into the bone from
open fractures and puncture wounds.4

With acute hematogenous osteomyelitis, patient presentation typically is within days to
weeks of initial symptoms; however, if acute osteomyelitis is unmanaged or
undermanaged, it can evolve into subacute and/or chronic osteomyelitis. Subacute
osteomyelitis is defined as an infection with a duration of more than 2 weeks without
acute symptomatology and often is of an insidious onset with mild symptoms.
Laboratory results often are normal, with negative blood cultures, normal white blood
cell count in 81% of patients, and normal CRP level in 52% of patients; however,
erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) greater than 20 mm/h is observed in 72% of
patients. Subacute osteomyelitis may result from incomplete management of acute
osteomyelitis, may occur in patients with prior antibiotic exposure, or may result from
bacteria that have a decreased virulence profile.16 A Brodie abscess is a subtype of
subacute osteomyelitis with a nidus of chronic infection contained within a sclerotic rim
of bone17 (Figures 1 and 2). Patients present with an insidious onset, mild symptoms,
and no systemic reaction. The complete classification of subacute osteomyelitis was
described by Gledhill18 and by Roberts et al.19
Type IA: metaphyseal radiolucency without surrounding sclerosis
Type IB: metaphyseal radiolucency with surrounding reactive bone
Type II: metaphyseal radiolucency with cortical erosion
Type III: cortical diaphyseal radiolucency with periosteal reaction
Type IV: diaphyseal lesion with subperiosteal new bone formation
Type V: epiphyseal radiolucency
Type VI: spine/vertebral lesion

Chronic osteomyelitis is relatively rare in the developed world and is far more common
in regions with limited access to medical care. If acute osteomyelitis goes unmanaged,
the infection can continue to spread beyond the cortex to form a subperiosteal abscess.
The underlying cortex is stripped of its blood supply and a necrotic region of bone,
termed a sequestrum, develops. This region acts as a reservoir for the infection and
cannot be penetrated by antibiotic agents. Over time, the surrounding periosteum
creates a thick sheath of new bone, termed the involucrum, and may eventually form a
draining sinus tract (Figure 3). The mainstay of the management of chronic infection is
surgical débridement20 (Resource 3).
Figure 3 Axial T2-weighted MRI of the tibia of a 4-year-old boy with chronic osteomyelitis
shows bone marrow edema and a soft-tissue abscess with a draining sinus tract.
(Courtesy of Erika Daley, MD, Royal Oak, MI, and Todd J. Blumberg, MD, Seattle, WA.)
CRMO, also known as chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis, was first described in 1972.
CRMO is a rare form of osteomyelitis that is caused by inflammation rather than an
infectious source. CRMO typically is associated with bone pain that is worse at night, may
or may not be associated with fevers, and is observed in otherwise well-appearing
children. CRMO typically affects the metaphysis of the lower extremities, and extra-
articular manifestations, such a skin rash; other associated auto-immune phenomenon
that may affect the gastrointestinal tract (celiac disease, ulcerative colitis); or kidney
disease are present in 25% of patients. CRMO is a diagnosis of exclusion, and often MRI

is defined by its chronic and/or recurrent course with periodic exacerbations. CRMO
typically is a self-limiting condition that improves over the course of years but can be
managed with the use of NSAIDs, tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors, or
diphosphonates21,22 (Resource 4).

Clinical Presentation
Patients with acute osteomyelitis often present with pain and localized symptoms, such as
warmth, erythema, swelling, reduced range of motion or weight bearing, and systemic
symptoms, such as fever, chills, and elevated heart rate.
Laboratory markers and vital signs should be closely evaluated for signs of systemic
inflammatory response syndrome.
The differential diagnosis for acute osteomyelitis includes eosinophilic granuloma, Ewing
sarcoma, soft-tissue abscess, and septic arthritis.

Clinical Presentation
The most common sign and symptom of osteomyelitis is pain (100% of patients) and
localized erythema (95% of patients).4 Local warmth (87% of patients), swelling (63% of
patients), reduced weight bearing (50% of patients), and reduced range of motion (50%
of patients) also are common.23 Newborns may present with pseudoparalysis of the
extremity. Generalized symptoms of a systemic inflammatory response, including fever,
chills, pallor, elevated heart rate, nausea/vomiting, and oliguria are observed in
approximately 50% of patients.4 Children with a severe presentation of osteomyelitis
may present with signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome and sepsis. The
normal ranges of vital signs vary by patient age. Pediatric systemic inflammatory
response syndrome is diagnosed if a patient meets two of the following criteria, one of
which must be an abnormal temperature or white blood cell count: abnormal
temperature (>101.3°F [38.5°C] or <98.8°F [36°C]), heart rate higher than two standard
deviations of normal for age or less than the 10th percentile for age if child is younger
than 1 year, respiratory rate higher than 2 standard deviations of normal for age, and
white blood cell count higher or lower than normal for age or more than10% immature
forms.24
In patients in their first two decades of life, the differential diagnosis for pain, fever, local
tenderness, and elevated inflammatory markers includes osteomyelitis; soft-tissue
abscess; myositis; septic arthritis; and tumors, including eosinophilic granuloma,
osteosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma. Advanced imaging studies are critical to distinguish

these diagnoses; however, the final diagnosis may require formal biopsy with pathologic
evaluation. Osteomyelitis and Ewing sarcoma may demonstrate a lamellated periosteal
reaction on radiographs and an adjacent soft-tissue mass on advanced imaging studies.
The histopathology of acute osteomyelitis demonstrates a field of polymorphonuclear
leukocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells (Figure 5). In eosinophilic granuloma,
pathology may demonstrate Langerhans cells with Birbeck granules and adjacent
inflammatory cells. Ewing sarcoma demonstrates pathognomonic small, round, blue
tumor cells.
Figure 5 Histologic image with hematoxylin-eosin stain shows acute suppurative
osteomyelitis. At right, necrotic trabecular bone features lacunae devoid of osteocytes.
The adjoining fatty marrow has been replaced by a polymorphous infiltrate of fibrin and
leukocytes, predominantly neutrophils. (Reproduced with permission from Pathorama,
Zurich, Switzerland.)
The diagnosis of subacute osteomyelitis may be particularly challenging and may mimic
several different diagnoses, particularly fractures, tumors, or malignancies (Figure 6).
Biopsy often is required to determine the definitive diagnosis. Associated cortical erosion
and periosteal reaction can be observed in patients with subacute osteomyelitis,
osteosarcoma, or Ewing sarcoma. Subacute osteomyelitis also may mimic osteoid

epiphyseal lesions may appear similar to chondroblastoma. The differential diagnosis for
a Brodie abscess may include intracortical hemangioma and stress fracture. The
presence of a draining sinus tract should confirm the diagnosis of a Brodie abscess.

Diagnosis
Radiographs often appear normal in the early stages of acute osteomyelitis, with changes not
appearing until several weeks from initial symptoms.
MRI can detect subtle bone marrow edema in the early stages of osteomyelitis with almost
100% sensitivity.
Laboratory studies, including ESR, CRP level, complete blood count, and blood cultures, are
included in the routine workup of suspected osteomyelitis.
Bone aspiration can be performed early in the disease course to identify a pathogen and to
evaluate for septic arthritis, subperiosteal abscess, and/or osteomyelitis.

Diagnosis
Plain radiographs often appear normal in the early stages of osteomyelitis. Bone loss of
30% to 40% is required before bone destruction is visible on radiographs; several weeks
from the time of initial infection often are required before such changes are observed on
radiographs. Changes in flat bones and the spine may take even longer to appear.
Radiographic findings associated with acute osteomyelitis include periosteal reaction
and elevation with a Codman triangle. Chronic osteomyelitis will demonstrate a
sequestrum (devitalized bone) with surrounding involucrum (new bone formation
associated with periosteal stripping) (Figure 7). A Brodie abscess will feature a
radiolucent region surrounded by a rim of sclerotic bone and may have a lucent channel
extending toward the epiphyseal plate. A Brodie abscess is most commonly observed in
the distal tibia metaphysis.

Figure 7 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the tibia of a 4-year-old boy with chronic
osteomyelitis demonstrate cortical thickening (arrow) consistent with involucrum
formation. (Courtesy of Erika Daley, MD, Royal Oak, MI, and Todd J. Blumberg, MD,

MRI is the most valuable advanced imaging study for the diagnosis of osteomyelitis. MRI
can detect subtle marrow changes in the very early phases of osteomyelitis with almost
100% sensitivity. The classic findings include changes in signal intensity because of
edema and increased water content within the marrow. T2-weighted and short tau
inversion recovery MRIs will appear bright and demonstrate increased signal intensity
because the fatty marrow is replaced by an inflammatory response (Figure 8). On T1-
weighted MRIs, marrow signal intensity is reduced and appears dark at the site of
osteomyelitis. If intravenous gadolinium is used, a bright rim of enhancement will be
observed surrounding a region of decreased density. The penumbra sign on an
unenhanced T1-weighted MRI is characteristic sign of subacute osteomyelitis with
abscess formation. A region of intermediate signal intensity forms a ring between the
infection cavity and the surrounding reactive bone, which appear as a lower intensity
signal (Figure 9). Intravenous gadolinium contrast does not improve the sensitivity or
specificity of MRI for the diagnosis of osteomyelitis compared with non–contrast-
enhanced MRI; however, it increases the confidence of the radiologist with regard to the
diagnosis of osteomyelitis, particularly in patients with an abscess.25

In addition, advanced imaging studies, such as CT or bone scintigraphy, may be
considered in select patients and if MRI is not readily available. CT may be used to
identify a soft-tissue abscess, which will appear as a heterogeneous collection with thick
margins that enhance with intravenous contrast. CT also may demonstrate gas adjacent
to fascial planes and decreased density of infected bone. Bone scintigraphy is no longer
used as a primary imaging modality for the diagnosis of osteomyelitis and has been
surpassed by MRI. It Bone scintigraphy most helpful if the site of infection is unclear,
such as with CRMO, or if multiple sites of infection are suspected and must be identified,
especially in patients with contraindication to MRI.26
Laboratory tests are a necessary part of the initial evaluation of patients with
osteomyelitis. CRP level and ESR are acute-phase response markers that are elevated in
the setting of inflammation and infection. ESR is an indirect measurement that may be
influenced by various factors. An ESR lower than 30 mm/h is considered normal. CRP
level is a direct measure of the acute phase response and tends to be elevated earlier
than ESR. A CRP level lower than 10 mg/L is considered normal. ESR and CRP level are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:38 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Osteomyelitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002081
16/33

important laboratory markers that are used to monitor patient response to treatment.
CRP levels typically peak within 48 hours of infection and may normalize within 1 week of
management. ESR, has a slower response, tending to peak approximately 3 to 5 days
after an infection begins and taking as long as 1 month to normalize. A complete blood
count with differential may be helpful and demonstrate an increase in the percentage of
polymorphonuclear leukocytes; however, a complete blood count is not always elevated,
particularly in children with subacute or chronic infections. Blood cultures should always
be obtained and yield a pathogen in more than 40% of pediatric patients with acute
hematogenous osteomyelitis.
Bone aspiration also is a useful tool in the early phase of diagnosis of osteomyelitis. By
obtaining different aspirations at the level of the periosteum and after puncturing the
cortex with a needle, the surgeon can evaluate for osteomyelitis and subperiosteal
abscess. The surgeon also should perform joint aspiration at the same time as bone
aspiration if septic arthritis also is suspected. Finally, bone aspiration also may help to
quickly identify a pathogen without the delay of formal biopsy.26
In younger children aged 6 months to 4 years, K kingae should be considered as the
causative organism. Because K Kingae is difficult to culture via standard means, bone
aspiration material should be plated on blood and chocolate agar to increase the
likelihood of isolation.
Management
The initial treatment of all children with acute infectious osteomyelitis is intravenous antibiotic
agents.
The choice of antibiotic agent is based on the patient’s clinical history and presentation and
unique risk factors (ie, history of MRSA, unvaccinated children, history of sickle cell anemia) but
should always include coverage for S aureus.
Vancomycin is used in children with a personal or family history of MRSA.
Response to management should be closely monitored via laboratory markers, vital signs,
patient history, and physical examination.

Surgical treatment is indicated in children who have a subperiosteal abscess, contiguous septic
arthritis, or fail to respond to empiric intravenous antibiotic agents.

Management
The mainstay of the initial management of pediatric osteomyelitis is intravenous
antibiotic agents. Historically, the administration of antibiotic agents has been delayed
until cultures were obtained because of concern about reducing the yield of cultures;
however, recent data have demonstrated that cultures are not affect by the timing of
antibiotic initiation and may be initiated early in the clinical course.27 Importantly,
antibiotic agents should not be withheld in children with signs and symptoms of sepsis,
including fevers, tachycardia, hypotension, and evidence of end-organ damage (such as
confusion, lethargy and oliguria). The choice of the initial antibiotic agent is guided by the
patient’s history and unique risk factors (Table 1). Initial antibiotic selection should
always include coverage for S aureus via an anti-staphylococcal ß-lactam antibiotic, such
as first-generation cephalosporin (ie, cefazolin) or, in patients with severe penicillin
allergy, clindamycin. Additional information regarding antibiotic mechanism of action,
adverse effects, and antimicrobial resistance is shown in Tables 2, 3, and 4 (Resource 1).

In children with a documented personal or family history of MRSA infection or in regions
in which CA-MRSA is endemic, intravenous clindamycin or vancomycin should be
included as a first-line treatment option. The efficacy of vancomycin against MSSA

infections is less than that of anti-staphylococcal ß-lactams and should be used only as
monotherapy after MRSA is confirmed. An algorithm for distinguishing MRSA from MSSA
osteomyelitis has identified four independent multivariate predictors of MRSA:
temperature higher than 100.4°F (38°C), hematocrit level less than 34%, white blood cell
count higher than 12,000 cells/μL, and CRP level higher than 13 mg/L. The probability of
MRSA osteomyelitis is 92% in children with all four predictors, 45% in children with three
predictors, 10% in children with two predictors, 1% in children with one predictor, and
zero in children with zero predictors.28
After the initiation of antibiotic agents, children should be closely monitored for
response. Laboratory markers, particularly CRP level, should be followed and should
downtrend in children who are appropriately responding to intravenous antibiotic
agents. Given the short half-life of CRP, CRP level is the best indicator of early
management success and should be expected to downtrend within 48 hours of
management.29 A child’s pain level, fever curve, CRP level trend, and physical
examination should improve over time, confirming resolution of infection. Finally, blood
cultures also should be serially drawn and should be remain negative as the infection
resolves. Patients can be transitioned to oral antibiotic agents and to complete therapy
after they have been afebrile for at least 24 hours, have had 48 hours of negative blood
cultures, and have substantially down-trending CRP levels with improved clinical
examination. The recommended duration of management is controversial, with
osteomyelitis typically requiring 4 to 6 weeks of management and MRSA osteomyelitis
requiring a minimum of 6 weeks of management. ESR should return to normal before
discontinuing antibiotic therapy. In children with chronic osteomyelitis, a prolonged
course of intravenous antibiotic agents, typically at least 3 months, often is
recommended. Laboratory studies can be monitored weekly to confirm complete
normalization of inflammatory markers and no systemic toxicity results from prolonged
antibiotic therapy.
Surgical management is considered in several clinical scenarios. In patients with a large
intraosseous or subperiosteal abscess, surgical drainage and thorough irrigation is
recommended to reduce bacterial load. Intraoperative cultures should be obtained, and
a drain should be placed. In children with radiographic evidence of chronic osteomyelitis
and a sequestrum, surgical débridement of necrotic bone often is necessary because

persistent elevation of inflammatory markers or bacteremia that fails to resolve after
empiric intravenous antibiotic agents, surgical treatment with intraoperative cultures is
indicated to direct antibiotic therapy. Although empiric management of acute
hematogenous osteomyelitis without associated subperiosteal abscess often is very
successful, surgeons must recognize if this strategy is not successful and proceed with
surgical management to better direct treatment (Video 1).

Complications
In children with a more severe clinical presentation of osteomyelitis, complications, such as
coagulopathy with deep vein thrombosis and septic pulmonary emboli, septic arthritis, and
multifocal osteomyelitis, must be anticipated.
Long-term complications of osteomyelitis include pathologic fracture and growth disturbance.

Complications
Children with a severe systemic inflammatory response secondary to disseminated
infection have an increased risk for complications. Children older than 8 years with
MRSA osteomyelitis and a CRP level higher than 60 mg/L on presentation have a 40% of
incidence of deep vein thrombosis. Pharmacologic prophylaxis should be considered in
children with a higher risk for thrombosis secondary to disseminated disease.
Septic arthritis as a concomitant infection in a child with osteomyelitis should not be
missed. Because intracapsular metaphyseal osteomyelitis can spread into the hip,
shoulder, ankle, and elbow joints, associated septic arthritis must be ruled out. In
addition, osteomyelitis in younger children, especially those younger than 18 months,
can spread via transphyseal vessels into the epiphysis and into any adjacent
articulations.
Acute hematogenous multifocal osteomyelitis must be considered in children with a
more severe clinical presentation. Multiple acute infections can occur in several bones
simultaneously via hematogenous seeding. These children have a higher risk of sepsis.
Importantly, osteomyelitis in neonates is multifocal in 40% of patients, and a high index
of suspicion must be maintained in these young patients who are unable to localize
pain.30
In children with severe acute, subacute, or chronic osteomyelitis, pathologic fractures
may occur as sequelae (Figure 10), complicating management and recovery. Soft-tissue
rest via short-term immobilization, protected–weight bearing, and activity modifications
should be considered in patients with osteomyelitis, especially those who undergo
substantial drainage procedures or multiple corticotomies.
Long term, patients with juxtaphyseal osteomyelitis should be monitored for growth
disturbances, including growth arrest with acquired limb-length discrepancy, and partial
growth arrest with resultant angular deformity. These children may require future
surgical treatment, particularly if physeal injury occurs, especially in the lower
extremities.
